keyTerms.definition: Cheapest knob and weakest; 2 hours of work.
Middle knob; changes behavior deeply, costs a training run.
Bigger model or more test-time calls; 3x inference cost forever.

recall.answer: Accuracy 0.72, bar 0.80. Rewrite prompt (2h), fine-tune small model (50 GPU-hours), or switch to big model (3x cost forever). Buy the cheapest accuracy first; per-query cost compounds over the product lifetime.

keyTerms.definition: Freezes the big matrix; learns a small detour B A.
r << min(d, k); the task's weight change must fit in rank r.
Any rank-r matrix factors as B A with r(d + k) numbers.

recall.answer: W' = W + B A with B 1024x8 and A 8x1024. Trainable numbers drop from 1,048,576 to 16,384. The base model knows language; the task needs a small steering change.
recall.question: How does LoRA shrink the update?

keyTerms.definition: Copies behavior, not weights; teacher labels data, student trains.
The teacher's probabilities; teaches which wrong answers were close.
Must be right often enough that its labels help.

recall.answer: Big model 0.90 at 10x cost; small model 0.75. Train the student on 1000 teacher-labeled examples. Soft targets (A 0.7, B 0.25, C 0.05) teach the boundary between answers.
recall.question: How does distillation work?

keyTerms.definition: Two stages: learn reward from pairs, then optimize policy with RL.
One stage: the optimal policy has a closed form; train directly on pairs.
Loss = -log sigma(beta m); beta sets how far the policy may move.

recall.answer: 1000 pairs (x, y_w, y_l), beta = 0.1. No reward model, no RL: train directly on w beats l. The loss rises when the model favors y_l over the reference, falls when it favors y_w.
recall.question: How does DPO skip the reward model?

keyTerms.definition: What the agent did; $0.01 each, noisy.
What an expert would do; $2 each, clean.
Whether the outcome was good; thumbs up/down.

recall.answer: Traces: automatic logs, $0.01 each, noisy. Demos: human performs the task, $2 each, clean. Feedback: thumbs up/down on outcomes. Mix: clone demos, learn preferences from feedback, filter traces.
recall.question: What are the three data sources?

keyTerms.definition: A printing press with a quality inspector.
Keep x when V(x) passes; works when V beats G.
Generation after generation with no fresh real data; variance collapses.

recall.answer: Generate 1000 examples with the big model; the verifier accepts 850; train on the 850. The loop works when the verifier is more accurate than the generator. The risk: inbreeding without fresh real data.
recall.question: How does synthetic data work?

keyTerms.definition: Deploy, collect, annotate, train, redeploy; the loop compounds.
u x f traces/day; 1000 users, 10% flagged, $2 each.
Flagged traces must be the informative ones.

recall.answer: 1000 users/day, 10% flagged, $2 per annotation. Daily yield: 100 traces. The two failure points: the collection rule and the annotation lag.
recall.question: How does the flywheel yield data?

keyTerms.definition: Triage for annotation; the 100 highest-uncertainty traces.
Train, score the pool, annotate the top-b, retrain.
The expensive step; selection makes it count.

recall.answer: Budget covers 100 of 10,000 traces. Random 100 teach what the model knows; the 100 with highest uncertainty teach the boundary. A confident-correct example has gradient near zero.
recall.question: Which 100 traces do you annotate?

keyTerms.definition: Quarantine; training teaches, eval judges.
Any path by which eval content reaches training.
A 13-gram shared between train and eval is near-certain copying.

recall.answer: 200 eval docs, 12 share a 13-gram with training: 6% leakage. The model scores 0.88 on leaked items vs 0.74 on clean ones. The inflation comes from memory, not ability.
recall.question: What does leakage do to the score?

keyTerms.definition: A scoring function: code, model judge, or human rubric.
Scores track reality: 0.8 means about 80% pass.
mean(v) - mean(h) on a calibration set.

recall.answer: 10 items; at threshold 0.5 the validator says all 10 pass but humans disagree. Calibrate before optimizing: the optimizer amplifies validator errors.
recall.question: Why calibrate before optimizing?

keyTerms.definition: The workbench: optimize freely; 1000 items.
The referee: score on a schedule, never tune; 200 items.
The vault: one look at the end; 200 items.

recall.answer: Dev (1000 items, touch freely), held-out test (200 items, score weekly), sealed (200 items, score once). Every peek at a higher tier leaks tuning signal into the number.
recall.question: What are the three tiers?

keyTerms.definition: Words to numbers to data; the U05 arc.
Traces, demos, feedback, synthetic data, flywheel.
Kept honest while optimizing (C10, C11, C12).

recall.answer: Prompt optimizers search wording, the tradeoff orders knobs, LoRA and distillation change weights cheaply, DPO trains on preferences, and the data half builds the training set while C10-C12 keep the eval honest.
